blocks.text: A resistor R and an inductor L are connected in series with an AC source V (Fig 17.10 a), so the same current I = Io sin(theta) flows through both. The rms voltage across R is VR = Irms R, in phase with the current (line OA in Fig 17.10 c). The rms voltage across L is VL = Irms XL, ahead of the current by 90 degrees (line OB). The resultant voltage V is their vector sum (line OP): Vrms = square root of (VR^2 + VL^2) = Irms square root of (R^2 + (wL)^2). So the impedance is Z = Vrms / Irms = square root of (R^2 + (wL)^2) (17.23), and the phase angle is theta = tan^-1(wL/R). Here the voltage leads the current by theta (Fig 17.10 b).

blocks.alt: Left: an RC series circuit (R and C in series with an AC source) and its voltage triangle: VR = IR along the current, VC = IXC pointing at right angles below it, and the resultant V = IZ; Z = sqrt(R^2 + (1/wC)^2), tan(theta) = XC/R. Right: an RL series circuit and its triangle with VL = IXL pointing at right angles above VR; Z = sqrt(R^2 + (wL)^2), tan(theta) = wL/R.
blocks.caption: RC and RL series circuits and their voltage triangles (original diagram after Figs 17.9 and 17.10).
blocks.long_description: The resistor's voltage is in step with the current; the capacitor's voltage is a quarter cycle behind and the inductor's a quarter cycle ahead. Pythagoras gives the total voltage, and the angle gives the phase difference.

blocks.text: Power in an RL series circuit

The power consumed is due to the resistor, because the inductor stores energy but ideally does not dissipate it: P = I^2 R = VI cos(theta). The factor cos(theta) is called the power factor. When DC power (for example from solar panels) is converted into AC power by an inverter, the inverter efficiency, usually 85 to 90 per cent, must be included: Pac = (inverter efficiency) x Pdc.
